md: Multi-query is not a magic recall knob. In our toy no phrasing ever retrieves d8, so even the full union of all lists tops out at recall 0.8. Multi-query can only find documents that some phrasing ranks within the per-query depth, the number of results each phrasing returns (5 here).

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Why one scorer cannot be both cheap and accurate
md: A reranker never finds anything. It can only reorder the list it receives. If stage 1 missed a document, no later stage, however large, can bring it back.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: The design space: ProphetNet to registers, and MTP in open models
md: Every MTP design asks a position about tokens further ahead; they differ in what that prediction may see (prefix only, or true tokens in between), where the parameters live (none, heads, a module, one embedding), and whether anything is kept for drafting. Joint training from pretraining beats bolting heads on later.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: SOAP: run Adam in the coordinates Shampoo discovers
md: SOAP is not cheap in memory. Per $m \times n$ layer it stores $L$, $Q_L$, $R$, $Q_R$, $M$, $V$ plus the gradient: $2m^2 + 2n^2 + 3mn$ numbers, the same as Distributed Shampoo, against $3mn$ for AdamW. For a $4096 \times 4096$ layer that is 117.4M versus 50.3M floats. Variants with a one-sided rotation and Adafactor's factored $V$ cut this to $2\min(m,n)^2 + 2mn$.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What breaks in SP after a single training step
md: Common misconception: "SP is broken only because the learning rate is too large for big models." Lowering it uniformly fixes the exploding layers but freezes others, such as the input embeddings. The issue is the *relative* scaling between layers.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Transferring across depth: branch multipliers, Depth-muP, CompleteP
md: A branch multiplier changes the model, not just its HPs. Pick $\alpha$ before tuning, use the same $\alpha$ and base depth in the proxy and the target, and keep the proxy deep enough that the depth rule is in its intended regime (EleutherAI's guide keeps the proxy's depth close to the target's for exactly this reason).

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: The futex: sleep on an address, wake by address
md: Returning from FUTEX_WAIT does not mean the lock is yours. The call can fail with EAGAIN, be interrupted by a signal (EINTR), or wake spuriously (return as if woken although no wake was meant for this lock), and another thread may grab the lock first. Always loop and re-check the word.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Read Committed vs Repeatable Read: when the snapshot is taken
md: Read Committed: new snapshot per statement, writers re-apply on top of concurrent commits. Repeatable Read: one snapshot per transaction, writers that hit a concurrent commit get error 40001 and must retry.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The metric: entity-level micro F1 with exact span match
md: Never report token accuracy for NER. CoNLL-2003 English training data holds one entity per 8.7 tokens, so the great majority of tags are O and a tagger that predicts O everywhere scores high token accuracy with an entity F1 of exactly zero. Entity-level micro F1 is the metric; token accuracy is a training diagnostic at best.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Write NSA and DSA as masked attention and test them against dense
md: Write the masked reference first. Setting the sparsity knob to select everything must reproduce dense attention exactly, and any fast kernel can then be compared with the reference on random inputs, including its gradients.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: One controller, many RL Actors: the NeMo RL architecture
md: NeMo RL separates *what the algorithm does* (a single-controller loop written as if on one GPU) from *where it runs* (RayVirtualCluster plus RayWorkerGroups). Swapping vLLM for another engine, or changing GPU counts, should not change the algorithm code.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: BGP hijacks and route leaks: the MyEtherWallet case
md: A BGP hijack does not need to touch your servers or your users' networks. It moves traffic somewhere else on the internet, where your TLS certificate, DNSSEC signatures and user training are the remaining defences.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Packets, flows and logs: three kinds of network evidence
md: Packets are the most complete evidence and the most expensive to keep. Logs and flows are what you will actually have for anything older than a few days, so design your monitoring around the questions you will need to answer months later.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Case: hunting Cobalt Strike servers by certificate, JARM and quirks
md: Hunt with layers: a cheap exact indicator (default serial, OpenSSL default subject), a fingerprint of the software (JA3S, JA4S, JARM), and behaviour (timing, rarity, newly seen servers). Each layer catches what the others miss, and corroboration turns leads into findings.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Ethernet frames and MAC addresses
md: A MAC address is not an identity. Operating systems let you change it, [Android](https://source.android.com/docs/core/connect/wifi-mac-randomization) uses a randomized address per Wi-Fi network by default since Android 10, and it never leaves the local link: routers replace it at every hop. "Allow only these MAC addresses" stops honest mistakes, not attackers.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Reading a packet capture like a defender
md: Captures contain other people's data: passwords, messages, cookies. Capture only on networks and machines you own or are explicitly authorised to monitor, keep the files protected, and delete them when done. Intercepting others' traffic without authorisation is illegal in most countries (the security basics course covers the law).

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Worked example: what placement costs in latency and bandwidth
md: Good NUMA placement does two things at once: it keeps misses local (latency) and it spreads traffic over every memory controller (bandwidth). Losing either one can cost more than the latency penalty alone suggests.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
md: NMS is not learned and does not look at the image. It only sees boxes and scores. It cannot remove a confident false positive that overlaps nothing (B3), and in dense scenes it removes real objects that happen to overlap.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Object storage is a strange kind of disk
md: Object storage is cheap, durable and shared, which makes compute stateless. The price is high per-request latency and a per-request fee. Everything else follows from batching writes and caching reads to pay that price rarely.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Inside a classic histogram: buckets, cumulative counts, interpolation
md: A classic histogram quantile is an interpolation inside one bucket. Its error is bounded by that bucket's width and nothing else, so a percentile panel is only as good as the boundary you placed next to the value you care about.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Reading a line: CRNN features and CTC decoding
md: CTC adds a blank symbol and a collapse rule (merge repeats, then drop blanks). That lets a recognizer train from whole-line transcripts with no character positions, and the blank is what makes double letters possible.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Discretionary vs mandatory access control, and the LSM hooks
md: MAC limits damage; it does not remove bugs. The SELinux Notebook is blunt: SELinux "will not stop memory leaks or buffer over-runs" and "will not stop kernel vulnerabilities", though it may contain their effects. A policy also cannot stop anything it allows.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Putting it together: one service, many layers
md: Assume each layer will fail and ask what the next one still guarantees: least privilege inside the program (privsep, drops), MAC around it, seccomp and capabilities on its kernel access, namespaces and cgroups around its view, and a separate kernel when the code is hostile. Patching is the layer under all of them.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Search operators: asking a search engine precise questions
md: Operators filter the search engine's copy, not the site. They are cheap and silent, which is why defenders should run them against themselves first.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Case: MH17 and the open-source trail of a missile launcher
md: MH17 is the model: geolocate each item, chronolocate it with independent methods, fingerprint the object, state the limits, and let formal investigators test it.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500
md: A common misconception is that editing a `.h` file only affects the `.cpp` with the same name. The compiler pastes headers into every includer, so `tensor.h` here costs 4 recompiles, not 1.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Running exactly the tests that matter with pytest
md: Node ids, `-k`, `-m` and `--lf` turn a 20 minute suite into a 2 second loop. Use the narrow loop while fixing, then run the wider set CI will run before you push.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Answering review comments as the author
md: Answer every comment, say what you changed, fix the code rather than explaining it in the thread, and thank the reviewer. The kernel guide adds: when you send a new version, list what changed since the previous one.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Codes of conduct: scope, reporting and the enforcement ladder
md: A CoC is not only about insults. Contributor Covenant 2.1 lists publishing others' private information (an address, an email) without explicit permission as unacceptable, and it covers private harassment too.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Folding review fixes into the right commit with --fixup
md: Fixup commits are not magic on their own. If you push `fixup!` commits and never autosquash, a PR merged with a merge commit or with rebase and merge (two of GitHub's merge methods, covered in lesson 5) lands them on main exactly as they are, `fixup!` titles and all. Autosquash before asking for the final merge unless the project says otherwise.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Copyleft: when you must share source, and with whom
md: Two common myths: copyleft does not make internal use public (only conveying triggers it), and it does not ban commercial use (you may charge for copies). What it controls is the terms you pass on.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: What a reviewer needs before merging a speedup
md: Common misconception: "the new number is smaller, so the change is faster". Two single measurements differ almost always, even for identical code. Without repeated runs and a test, a 5% gap can be pure noise.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Trace one request: a Redis GET from socket to reply
md: Trace from the specific end toward the general one. Start at the observable string or the command's own handler, search downward through callees, and use a backtrace (or a log line) to bridge function pointers, callbacks and event loops.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: git bisect: finding the commit that introduced the bug
md: Do not reuse a reducer's interestingness script as a bisect script unchanged. They use opposite conventions: for C-Reduce and llvm-reduce, exit 0 means the bug is *present*; for `git bisect run`, exit 0 means the commit is *good* (bug absent). The inversion silently sends bisect to the wrong commit.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: A title and description that explain why
md: Do not write `Closes #123` on a PR that only partly addresses the issue: merging it will close the issue for everyone. Write "Part of #123" or "Refs #123" (neither is a closing keyword).

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Automatic prefix caching in vLLM: hashing full blocks
md: Only **full** blocks are cached. If two prompts share 10 tokens and the block size is 16, nothing is reused. Lookup also always starts from block 0: a shared passage in the middle of two prompts gives no hit, because its KV depends on everything before it.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Passive recon: certificate logs, search engines and leaked code
md: A leaked password or API key found during recon is not an invitation to log in with it. Unless the rules of engagement explicitly allow using discovered credentials, record where it was found and report it at once so it can be rotated.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
md: Colors carry no meaning in a default CPU flame graph. Gregg picks random warm colors only to separate neighbors. Other palettes exist (for example coloring kernel, user and just-in-time (JIT) frames differently, where JIT code is machine code that a runtime such as the Java virtual machine compiles while the program runs), but never read hotness from hue.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Flushes, fences and the order things become durable
md: A fence without a flush does nothing for durability on ADR platforms, and a flush without a fence gives no ordering: CLWB and CLFLUSHOPT are not ordered with each other or with later stores. You need both, in the order store, flush, fence, then the dependent store.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: DMARC: alignment, policy and reports
md: Misconception: "we have DMARC, so we are protected from phishing". DMARC at p=reject stops exact-domain spoofing of **your** domain. It does nothing against lookalike domains, display-name spoofs or a compromised real mailbox, and p=none stops nothing at all; it only reports.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Shrinking a struct by reordering its fields
md: Do not reorder blindly. If a struct's layout is part of a file format, a network protocol, a hardware register map or an ABI shared with other code, changing the order changes the bytes and breaks every reader. Reordering is safe only for structs that are private to one build of your program.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Heatmaps: training targets, argmax and sub-pixel decoding
md: The network never outputs coordinates. It outputs heatmaps, and a small hand-written decoder (argmax, quarter-cell shift, scale by stride, undo the crop) turns them into numbers. Bugs in that decoder, such as swapping x and y or forgetting the crop offset, look like a bad model.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Encrypting one bit with LWE, by hand
md: This toy exists to make the math visible. Never write your own lattice cryptography for real use: use ML-KEM from a maintained library (lesson 8), whose implementers also handle constant-time code, input checks and randomness.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
md: Do not read 3% as a safe threshold. Proximity graphs are not random graphs, matching nodes are often clustered, and being connected is weaker than being *navigable*: greedy search can stall in a matching region long before the subgraph formally splits. Qdrant's docs simply warn that the HNSW graph starts to fall apart when filters are too strict.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: What privacy engineering protects, beyond keeping secrets
md: "Encrypted, access-controlled and never breached" is a security result, not a privacy result. A system can meet every confidentiality control and still harm people through what it does by design with the data: publishing, combining, inferring or keeping it.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: k-anonymity: generalise and suppress until you hide in a crowd
md: k-anonymity: every combination of quasi-identifier values appears at least k times, achieved by generalising and suppressing. Its strength depends entirely on choosing the right quasi-identifiers and on every other release made from the same data.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy in real systems: units, trust and hazards
md: Check every DP claim for its unit of privacy (event or user), its trust model (central, local or in between), its epsilon and delta (delta at most 1 / n squared), and its implementation (a vetted library, not hand-written noise).

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Secure aggregation: a server that learns only the sum
md: Secure aggregation: pairwise masks that cancel in the sum hide each value from the server; secret sharing handles dropouts; double masking stops a server from faking dropouts. The total is still revealed, so require many contributors and add DP noise when the total must not identify anyone.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 2: jobs, scripts and paths that root trusts
md: The same rule covers the files that define privilege themselves. A writable `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/sudoers.d/` entry or systemd unit directory is instant root. Treat any group or world write bit under `/etc` or `/usr` as a finding.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Build it: train a small PRM and rerank with it
md: Tokenize each step separately and append the separator id yourself. In the Qwen2.5 tokenizer a step ending in a period followed by a newline becomes the single token for period-plus-newline (id 624), so tokenizing the joined text gives no separate newline token to read, and the label would sit on a different token than at training time.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: What a process owns and what a thread shares
md: A process is a **resource container** (memory, files, handlers); a thread is an **execution stream** (PC, registers, stack). Threads in one process see each other's writes; separate processes do not, unless they set up sharing on purpose.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
md: The one number to remember is not the microseconds of a single switch but **switches per second times total cost per switch**, where total includes the cache and TLB refill. Keep CPU-bound threads near the core count, and reserve extra threads or async I/O for work that actually waits.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Worked example: selecting a prompt and the winner's curse
md: The data that chose the prompt cannot also grade it. Report the selected prompt's score on a held-out set that played no part in any choice, and expect it to be lower than the dev score.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Text versus bytes: what a computer actually stores
md: Do not "fix" decode errors with `errors="ignore"` in security tooling. It silently deletes the bad bytes, so `ad\xffmin` becomes `admin` and your report shows a username the attacker never sent. Prefer `replace`, which leaves a visible mark.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Encodings: base64, hex and URL encoding, and why attackers use them
md: Never decode and then *run* what you decoded to see what it does. Decode to text, read it, and search it. Executing an unknown PowerShell or shell command, even in your own terminal, is how an analyst becomes the next victim. Use an isolated analysis sandbox if you truly need behaviour.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Relevance feedback: Rocchio, pseudo-relevance feedback and RM3
md: Feedback is only as good as its top k. When the first-pass top results are relevant, PRF finds words the user never typed; when they are off-topic, it amplifies the error. On MS MARCO dev, the query2doc paper reports BM25 MRR@10 18.4 against 15.8 for BM25 + RM3, while recall@1k rose slightly (85.7 to 86.4).

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs
md: The rotation does not make every vector quantize well on every draw. It makes the quality *random with a known distribution*, the same for every input direction. That is what turns "works on my dataset" into a guarantee that holds regardless of the data.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Discounts, refunds and rewards: value that can be claimed twice
md: Evaluate every reward rule against the final state of the transaction, at the moment value moves, and record each grant so it cannot be granted again. A rule checked earlier is a rule that can go stale.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Fixing races in the database: atomic updates, locks, constraints
md: "It is in a transaction" is not a race fix by itself. At Read Committed, a SELECT then an UPDATE in one transaction still race. You need a lock, a conditional write, a constraint, or SERIALIZABLE with retries.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Why replicas need consensus, and why majorities work
md: Majorities intersect. Every safety argument in Paxos and Raft comes down to one server that sat in both quorums and remembered what it saw.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Top-k, the token budget, and where chunks sit in the prompt
md: Three separate decisions shape the context: **how many** chunks (top-k), **how many tokens** they may use (the budget, set by the window minus everything else), and **in what order** they appear. Tune them together; raising k without a budget or an ordering rule mostly adds noise to the middle.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Cutoff metrics and the divisors hidden inside them
md: **Recall@k is not Success@k.** Some papers report "Recall@k" meaning *at least one relevant document is in the top k*. The ir_measures documentation calls that **Success@k** and reserves R@k for the fraction of all relevant documents retrieved. For q1 every run has Success@5 = 1, while R@5 ranges from 0.167 to 0.667. Check which one a paper means before comparing numbers.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Extortion layers: encryption, theft, leak sites and pressure
md: Backups defeat encryption only. Stolen data is lost the moment it leaves, so treat exfiltration detection as part of ransomware defence, and prepare the communication that answers a leak-site post before one appears.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Recovery sequencing: identity first, then the business
md: Recover in dependency order: a clean network, then the independent backup system, then identity restored in isolation from a pre-attack backup with privileged secrets reset, then security tooling, then business services by a critical asset list agreed before the incident.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: WebSocket: one HTTP upgrade, then a two-way framed stream
md: Masking is **not encryption**: the key travels in the same frame. RFC 6455 requires it (even over TLS) so that a script in the browser cannot choose the exact bytes on the wire. Without it, an attacker could craft upgraded traffic that a broken proxy reads as an HTTP request and caches, then serves that forged response to other users: the cache-poisoning attack in section 10.3. Use `wss://` (TLS) for confidentiality.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
md: Item-to-item CF scales because the heavy work (the similar-items table) is offline, and the online step only touches the handful of items in one user's history.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why a photo has no scale until you add a reference
md: A reference object gives you scale only for points at its depth (more precisely, on its plane). Everything else in the image has a different pixels-per-mm.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
md: The same study found that most of PostgreSQL's timeouts came from a nested-loop join without an index, chosen because a tiny row estimate made it look cheapest. When the real input was large, its rows x rows work exploded. A cost-only choice ignores how risky a plan is if the estimate is wrong.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
md: The reward is an imperfect measurement of the goal. Optimization pressure flows to wherever the measurement and the goal disagree, so the harder you optimize, the more those disagreements decide what you get.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: From gaming to tampering: reward tampering and in-context hacking
md: Gaming generalizes. A model rewarded for easy, harmless-looking gaming became more likely to try rarer and more blatant gaming it was never trained on, and training away only the gaming you can see leaves some of the rest.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Monte Carlo: simulating 100,000 years of losses
md: Monte Carlo is not magic: garbage ranges give precise-looking garbage. The model also assumes the factors are independent (here, a bad attack year does not make secondary losses bigger), which may not hold. Show your inputs with the outputs, say what is assumed, and rerun when estimates change. Simplified: real FAIR tools also model multiple loss forms separately and correlations between factors.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: ISO/IEC 27001: an ISMS, Annex A and the certification audit
md: ISO 27001 certifies a management system: risk assessment, treatment, a Statement of Applicability against 93 Annex A controls, internal audit, management review, continual improvement. Certificates last three years with yearly surveillance. The SoA and your risk register are the documents everything else hangs from.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Breach notification clocks and US disclosure rules
md: Know your clocks before the incident: NIS2 24 h and 72 h, GDPR 72 h from awareness, SEC four business days from a materiality decision made without unreasonable delay, state laws often 30 to 60 days, HIPAA at most 60 days. Encryption is an exemption almost everywhere. Prepare templates and decision owners in the incident plan.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: One RL step is five workloads on two kinds of engine
md: Rollout is the bottleneck. FLOPs are dominated by training, but wall-clock time is dominated by sequential decoding. Most RL infrastructure ideas (fast inference engines, placement, resharding, asynchrony, partial rollouts) are ways to make generation faster or to keep the other GPUs busy while it runs.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: The roofline: attainable FLOP/s versus intensity
md: The ridge point tells you how hard the machine is to feed. The paper notes that a ridge far to the right means only kernels with very high intensity can reach peak. From the V100, NVIDIA's 2017 data center GPU (125 TFLOP/s of Tensor Core math over about 900 GB/s, a ridge of 138.9), to the H100 in BF16 (295.4), the ridge more than doubled.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Trigger, proximate cause, contributing factors, action items
md: The one thing to keep: triage narrows, mitigation buys time, and the postmortem is where the next incident gets cheaper. Each of the three uses a different artifact: the dependency graph and the distributions for narrowing, a rehearsed rollback or kill switch for mitigating, and a list of named conditions with owners for not doing it again.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: When score fusion beats RRF
md: Tuning RRF is not free robustness. Bruch et al. found that per-list constants tuned in-domain generalized poorly out-of-domain (HotpotQA fell from 0.675 to 0.621), while a convex combination's single α transferred well. If you tune, validate on traffic that looks like production.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: C calls Rust: a misc device from open() to ioctl()
md: Direction matters at the boundary: Rust calling C uses `to_result`/`from_err_ptr`; C calling Rust uses a trampoline that returns `err.to_errno()`. Ownership crossing the boundary goes through `into_foreign` once and `from_foreign` once.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run
md: Stashing a task in a BPF map from `select_cpu` does not skip `enqueue`; only a DSQ insertion does. The docs call storing tasks from `select_cpu` racy and discouraged. Also, the core ignores an invalid CPU choice such as one outside the task's allowed cpumask (the set of CPUs a task may run on, set with `sched_setaffinity()`).

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Keeping tasks in BPF: custody, dequeue and user-space policy
md: Misconception: once a task is in a custom DSQ it is on its way to a CPU. It is in your custody until dispatch moves it, and a property change can pull it back out through `ops.dequeue()` at any time.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Vaults: one place to store, control and audit secrets
md: A vault concentrates risk. CircleCI was, in effect, a vault for its customers' deploy secrets. Narrow policies per workload, short-lived tokens, audit logs shipped elsewhere, the ability to seal fast, and a root of trust in a KMS or HSM are what make the concentration worth it.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Taint by hand: following one value from source to sink
md: Trace by hand: mark the source, follow every assignment and call, and stop at each sink. A function only counts as a sanitizer if its output is safe for that specific sink, whatever the input. Rewriting or deleting bad patterns almost never qualifies.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Log4Shell as a review miss: a logger that interpreted its input
md: Parameterising user data protects you only if the component never interprets the final string. When reviewing a feature that adds interpretation (lookups, templates, expressions, fetching URLs) to a widely used API, treat every caller's data as reaching that new sink.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Memory-safe roadmaps: CISA's guidance and Android's numbers
md: Memory-safety policy is now a review topic: new memory-unsafe code needs a reason, unsafe blocks in Rust get the most scrutiny, and old C and C++ keeps its hardening. Android's data says the payoff comes from new code, because vulnerabilities concentrate in recent changes.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: SSH's transport layer: version, KEXINIT, key exchange and host keys
md: Everything in the KEXINIT lists is negotiated in the clear and only later authenticated through the exchange hash. Anything the hash does not cover (extra messages, the implicit sequence numbers) is a place where an active attacker can interfere.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Biba and integrity: no read down, no write up
md: Confidentiality: no read up, no write down. Integrity: no read down, no write up. If you remember which way information is allowed to flow, you can rebuild both rule sets.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Identity-aware proxies and ZTNA versus the VPN
md: A proxy only protects an application if it is the only way in and the application can tell the difference. Signed, audience-bound assertions let the application check for itself.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Rate limits, backoff with jitter, and partial failure
md: Pace all workers with one shared limiter, honour Retry-After and the reset headers, back off exponentially with full jitter, retry only idempotent calls and only at one layer, and report partial failures item by item.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: What security protects: assets and the CIA triad
md: A hash only proves integrity if the expected fingerprint reached you over a channel the attacker cannot touch. If an attacker can change both the message and the published hash, the check passes. Fixing that needs authenticity: a digital signature (or a keyed hash) that only the real sender can produce. The cryptography course covers these.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Scoring and prioritising: CVSS, KEV and EPSS
md: CVSS = how bad in theory. KEV = being used now. EPSS = likely to be used soon. Combine them with what *your* asset is and how exposed it is. A score without context is not a priority.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The legal and ethical line: authorisation and disclosure
md: Rules of thumb that keep you on the right side: test only systems you own or have written permission to test; stay inside the agreed scope (systems, dates, methods); stop and report the moment you see other people's data; never keep or share it. A bug bounty programme's published rules are a form of written permission, but only for what they list.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Getting a fix shipped when you cannot order it
md: Escalation is not a weapon. If owners learn that talking to security means being reported upward, they stop talking to security, and you lose the early warnings that matter most. Agree the path in advance, use it predictably, and make the first step always a direct conversation.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Build a STaR loop: sample, filter, fine-tune, repeat
md: Measure the filter, not just the score. Two cheap audits caught what accuracy alone hid: check an intermediate quantity on a sample of kept data, and track held-out accuracy every iteration, since training accuracy rises regardless.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Choosing the threshold: hit rate against false hits
md: Do not copy a threshold from a tutorial or a library default. Collect a few hundred real pairs from your traffic, label whether the cached answer would be correct, and pick the threshold from that data and your cost of a wrong answer. Re-check whenever you change the embedding model, since similarity scales differ between models.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Validating outbound URLs in code
md: Validate the *destination*, not the *string*: fixed scheme, allowlisted host, resolved IP checked against private ranges, the connection pinned to that IP, and no automatic redirects. Then assume the check will one day fail and limit what the network lets the server reach.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Cache-aware scheduling: queue order sets the hit rate
md: Greedy longest-prefix-first can **starve** a request whose prefix is never cached: requests that hit keep jumping ahead of it. The paper says so directly and leaves fair cache-aware scheduling as future work. Watch tail latency (the latency of the slowest requests, such as the 99th percentile) if you enable `lpm`.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
md: A* is Dijkstra with key g + h. Never overestimate (admissible) and you keep optimality; satisfy the triangle inequality (consistent) and each node is settled once. The closer h is to the true remaining cost, the fewer nodes settle.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: IIR filters, zero-phase filtering and real sensor data
md: Pick the filter by the job: moving average to smooth in time, windowed-sinc FIR (firwin) for clean band separation with linear phase, Butterworth IIR (as SOS) for a cheap sharp cutoff. Offline, filter forward and backward to cancel the delay.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Arm Neon and SVE: fixed width versus length agnostic
md: Neon is fixed 128-bit SIMD. SVE is vector-length agnostic: 128 to 2048 bits (a power of two), chosen by the chip. Predicates from whilelt make the tail just another iteration, so one binary scales across vector lengths.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Three modules, one loop: how slime is laid out
md: slime is a thin layer: Ray places the workers, SGLang generates, Megatron trains, and slime owns the glue in between (the Data Buffer, the rollout function and weight sync). Most behavior you might want to change is a command-line flag or a function path, not a fork.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: The alert lifecycle, and why the queue is not first come, first served
md: Allow-listing the scanner fixes the noise but creates a blind spot: an attacker on that address is now invisible to the rule. The NCSC says allow lists must be "strongly object/time bounded" (one address, its scheduled window, an expiry date) "to minimise the risk of perpetual allow listing and the evasion of monitoring".

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Cloud key misuse, and what Snowflake customers could see in 2024
md: Cloud and SaaS triage starts with three questions: what kind of credential is this, where is it being used from compared with normal, and what did it touch. The third question can only be answered if the right logs (S3 data events, the warehouse's query history) were switched on and kept long enough before the incident.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Password and MFA friction: rules that backfire and rules that work
md: Misconception: "more password rules means more security". Composition rules and forced changes make people choose predictable variants and write them down. Length, a blocklist, rate limiting, and MFA that is bound to the site do the real work.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Testing the people layer: rules of engagement, ethics and metrics
md: Test processes, not people. Authorise every site with whoever controls it, plan for police, review lures for harm, report without names, and measure reporting speed and procedure compliance rather than click counts.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
md: A latent dying is not the same as a feature being absent from the model. It only means this SAE found no use for that column, often because of optimisation, not because the concept is missing.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
md: Every interpolator here is a weighted average $\sum_i \lambda_i z_i$. The only question is how to pick the weights. Keep this frame: the rest of the course compares weight recipes on the same six sensors.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
md: Kriging is the best linear unbiased predictor (linear: a weighted sum of readings; unbiased: weights sum to 1; best: smallest error variance) only under its own model. With few points, an unreliable variogram can make it worse than IDW, as in this toy. Its variance map is only as trustworthy as the variogram, so check calibration with standardized LOO errors.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: EAGLE drafts, prompt lookup, and speculation in vLLM
md: All variants share one loop: draft cheaply (small model, extra heads, feature-level head, or string lookup), verify a chain or tree in one target pass, keep the accepted prefix plus one target token. They differ only in how they guess, and that sets alpha and c.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The map of a process: segments, /proc/PID/maps and ASLR
md: A big line in `/proc/PID/maps` is not memory in use. A VMA only says which addresses the program may touch; Linux's memory concepts docs note that anonymous mappings usually just define those areas, and physical pages arrive on first access. A 1 GiB mapping that was never written uses almost no RAM.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Walking an x86-64 page table, bit by bit
md: A miss does not always cost four DRAM reads. The page-table entries are ordinary data that can sit in the CPU caches, and Linux's page-table docs note that MMUs also keep page walk caches for upper levels. The four loads are the worst case of the structure, not a fixed latency.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Steering by adding a vector to the residual stream
md: A steering vector edits **activations**, not weights and not the prompt. It is computed once, before inference, and the same vector is added on every forward pass while it is switched on.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
md: Per-partition order is *write* order, not event-time order. If sensor A's readings were written late (e12 in our toy), they sit in the log after newer ones. Kafka removes the network chaos between bridge and processor, but it cannot undo disorder that happened before the write.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Why recurrence was the bottleneck for sequence models
md: Attention did not start with the Transformer. Additive attention over RNN states dates to Bahdanau et al. (2014). What was new in 2017 was using attention *alone*, with no recurrence or convolution.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Relative positions: from sinusoids to RoPE and ALiBi
md: Relative schemes put the offset m - n into the score itself. RoPE rotates queries and keys so their dot product depends only on content and offset; ALiBi subtracts a fixed per-head penalty proportional to distance. Neither adds anything to the input embeddings.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Document length normalization: what b controls
md: b = 1 is not "more correct". It assumes every long document is just verbose. For collections where long documents genuinely cover more (manuals, books split into chapters), strong normalization buries them. The survey reports that values around 0.5 < b < 0.8 work well in many settings, with optimal values depending on the documents and queries.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Assemble model.py and check it against GPT-2's real weights
md: Before training a from-scratch model, load the released GPT-2 weights into it and compare logits against a reference on a fixed prompt. A difference of zero (or float noise) proves the architecture; anything visibly larger means a wrong layer, a missing transpose or a different activation.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Derivative rules and the chain rule for nested functions
md: Chain rule: the derivative of a pipeline is the **product of the local derivatives** of its stages, each evaluated at the value that stage actually saw. Backpropagation is this rule applied systematically.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Second derivatives, the Hessian and the shape of a minimum
md: Positive diagonal entries do not make a minimum. $x^2 + 4xy + y^2$ has diagonal 2 and 2, but along $x = -y$ it equals $-2x^2$ and curves down: its Hessian's eigenvalues are 6 and -2, a saddle. Mixed partials can overturn what the axes suggest.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
md: Quote every expansion (`"$f"`, `"$(cmd)"`, `"$@"`) unless you specifically want splitting and globbing. Unquoted is the exception you choose, not the default.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
md: pipefail meets SIGPIPE: with pipefail on, `yes | head -n 1` has status 141, because yes was killed when head exited. `seq 1 3 | head -n 1` (seq prints the numbers 1 to 3) returns 0 only because all its output fit in the pipe before head quit. Under `set -e`, a producer piped into `head` can end the script on large inputs; test such pipelines at realistic sizes.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Train word2vec yourself: SGNS in PyTorch, then gensim
md: gensim's default is `sg=0`, which trains **CBOW**, not skip-gram, and its default `sample` is `1e-3`. Leaving the defaults in place trains a different model from the one in the paper you are reproducing. Always set `sg` explicitly.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
md: More cores does not mean every program runs faster. If each operation reads a lot of data and does little math per byte, the SMs wait on HBM no matter how many there are. The next lesson turns this into a number.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
md: A **program** is a file of bytes on disk. A **process** is a running instance of it: its own memory (code, data, heap, stack), its own register values (the CPU's working slots, lesson 3), and OS bookkeeping such as open files. One program can be running as many processes at once.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
md: `call` = push return address + jump. `ret` = pop into the program counter. Everything a function keeps on the stack lives only until it returns, which is why the stack can be reused so cheaply.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From text predictor to assistant: the three-stage recipe
md: Same network, three different training signals: raw text (what comes next?), demonstrations (what would a good assistant write?), and comparisons (which of these two answers is better?). Each stage starts from the weights of the previous one.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Where preference data comes from: guidelines, safety, AI feedback
md: AI feedback moves the specification, it does not remove it. The labels are only as good as the feedback model and the principles, and a model judging a model can share its blind spots. Teams still check AI-labeled preferences and the resulting policy against human judgments.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
md: Intersection is a linear merge over sorted lists. Make it cheap by starting from the rarest term, and make long lists skippable.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
md: A header declaring a function is not the same as the function existing. `#include` only pastes a promise into your file. If the definition lives in `area.c` (or a library), it must also reach the linker, or the build fails at link time with an undefined symbol error even though every file compiled cleanly.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Integer types and conversions: where -1 > 0u
md: Never compare a signed value with an unsigned one without thinking about negatives. `if (len < cap)` with `int len = -1` and `size_t cap = 16` is false on LP64 systems: len converts to a huge size_t. Keep lengths and indexes in size_t throughout, or check for negatives before comparing.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Files and errors: stdio, return codes and errno
md: Do not test errno to find out whether a call failed. A successful call may leave errno nonzero from some earlier, unrelated failure, or even set it itself. Test the return value; consult errno only after the return value reports failure.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
md: Ownership is not about the stack versus the heap as such. A `String` header can live on the stack, in a `Vec` (Rust's growable array), or inside a struct field; wherever it lives, that location is the owner, and the heap block is freed when that owner is dropped.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Structs that borrow: lifetimes in types and what 'static means
md: `T: 'static` does not mean the value lives forever. An owned `String` satisfies the bound and is still dropped at the end of its owner's scope. The bound only says the receiver may keep the value as long as it likes, because nothing inside it can dangle. `thread::spawn` puts this bound on its closure (lesson 10).

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
md: A dot product of 0 does not mean the vectors are unrelated in every sense; it means they are **perpendicular** (orthogonal). And a big dot product does not by itself mean similar direction: it can come from long vectors. When you want direction only, normalize first or use cosine.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Orthogonality, projections and least squares
md: Orthogonal matrices keep lengths and angles, and $Q^{-1} = Q^\top$. Projecting $\mathbf{b}$ onto a line or a column space leaves a residual orthogonal to it, and that orthogonality condition, $X^\top(\mathbf{y} - X\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{0}$, is least squares.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
md: The loss you minimize is computed on the **training** data, but what you actually care about is performance on new data. Lessons 6 to 9 show how these two come apart, and what to do about it.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Overfitting: when the training loss lies
md: Zero training error is not proof of a good model, and not proof of a bad one either. The degree-9 fit has zero training error and poor test error; lesson 9 shows that large modern networks can also hit zero training error and still generalize.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Data pitfalls: leakage, distribution shift and baselines
md: Fit everything (scalers, feature selection, imputation) inside the training fold, ideally with a Pipeline. Split by group or by time when rows are related. Expect distribution shift in deployment, and always report a trivial baseline next to your model.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Multi-class outputs: softmax, logits and the p minus y gradient
md: Misconception: raising one logit only raises its own probability. The Jacobian's off-diagonal entries $-p_i p_j$ are negative, so every other probability falls (they must still sum to 1). That is why a wrong class's logit gets the positive gradient $p_j$ even though the loss $-\ln p_y$ reads only the true class: $p_y$ depends on every logit through the softmax denominator.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
md: A system call is not just a function call. It looks like one because the C library wraps it, but inside is a trap that changes privilege level, and the kernel, not the caller, decides which code runs.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Waiting for something: condition variables and semaphores
md: A condition variable has no memory: signaling when nobody waits does nothing. That is why the waiting thread must check a state variable before it sleeps, rather than relying on catching the signal.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Describing data: mean, median, percentiles and outliers
md: Percentiles do not average. The p99 of two servers combined is not the mean of their two p99 values: it depends on how many requests each served and on the shape of both tails. Compute percentiles from the merged raw data (or from merged histograms).

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Continuous variables: densities, CDFs and common distributions
md: A density value is not a probability. A density of 2 does not mean probability 2, and the probability of any single exact value is 0, which is why $<$ and $\le$ give the same answer for continuous variables.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayesian estimation: priors, posteriors and MAP
md: Prior plus data gives a posterior. MAP is maximum likelihood plus a log-prior term, which is why L2 and L1 penalties are Gaussian and Laplace priors in disguise.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Fixed budget, best split: IsoFLOP curves
md: Compute-optimal training scales model size and data **together**, each roughly as the square root of compute. The rule of thumb that falls out is about 20 training tokens per parameter.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Precision, recall, and why accuracy is useless for search
md: P@k does not average well across queries. If a query has only 3 relevant documents, even a perfect system gets P@10 = 0.3. Also note that trec_eval's P@k pads short result lists with nonrelevant documents: retrieving 15 documents with 4 relevant gives P@20 = 4/20 = 0.2.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: From token vectors to one sentence vector: pooling and cosine
md: Pooling a pretrained language model does not give you a good embedding model. BERT was never trained to make cosine meaningful; the training objective in the next lesson is what does that.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
md: Ties are common on small data. This code picks the pair it encountered first, so a different tie-break or a different word order can produce a different merge list. Real trainers fix a deterministic rule; production implementations also update pair counts incrementally instead of recounting everything, as Sennrich et al. note.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: WordPiece, Unigram and SentencePiece in depth
md: BPE replays merges in learned order. WordPiece scores merges by count(ab) / (count(a) count(b)) and encodes by longest match. Unigram prunes a big vocabulary by likelihood and segments with Viterbi. SentencePiece runs BPE or Unigram on raw text with the space as a symbol.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Batch size, gradient accumulation and tuning hyperparameters
md: Batch size sets the speed; the learning rate decides whether you train at all. Tune the learning rate first, on a log scale: a range test finds the decade, random trials refine it. When you accumulate gradients, divide each micro-batch loss by the number of micro-batches.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Tuning ef and M, and choosing between HNSW, IVF and PQ
md: Tune HNSW in this order: pick M for your data (12 to 48 is typical), set ef_construction high enough that build-time recall is near 1, then sweep ef at query time against brute-force ground truth until recall@k meets your target at acceptable latency.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Signing artifacts: from long-lived keys to Sigstore
md: Verifying 'signed by somebody' proves nothing: an attacker can get a valid Sigstore certificate for their own identity in seconds. The security comes from `--certificate-identity` and `--certificate-oidc-issuer`, which you must set to the one workflow or person you actually expect.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Reproduce collapse yourself: simulate the loops, measure diversity
md: Three of these metrics only look inside the generated set: a generator can be varied in phrasing while missing whole topics. Only rare-slice coverage compares against real data, so keep a held-out real set. Also compare sets of equal size and length; distinct-n falls as texts get longer even with no loss of diversity, and 5-sentence sets like these are noisy.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: vdso(7) states that calls served by the vDSO do not appear in `strace` output (strace is a tool that prints every system call a process makes) and are invisible to seccomp filters (seccomp, secure computing mode, lets a process restrict which system calls it may make). A trace with zero `clock_gettime` lines does not mean the program never asks for the time.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Shared memory between processes: MAP_SHARED, shm_open and memfd
md: The ring spins while it waits, burning a whole CPU. Real shared-memory queues sleep when empty or full, for example on a POSIX semaphore placed in the shared region, as shm_overview(7) suggests, and use spinning at most for a short time first.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Coordinated omission: the load tester stops looking when it hurts
md: Coordinated omission does not make individual samples wrong: the 2 ms readings were real. The bug is which samples exist. The tester samples less often precisely when the server is slow, so the sample set is biased toward good moments. No statistic computed afterwards can recover samples that were never taken.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Let the LLM parse and let code do the date math
md: Let the LLM do language: extract date strings and turn query phrases into structured fields. Let code do time: normalize against an explicit reference date, merge, clip and compare. The result is exact, testable and the same on every run.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
md: The best use of test-time compute depends on the prompt. Search is most valuable where the model is weak but not hopeless; on easy prompts it can hurt by exploiting the verifier.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
md: TTT here does not mean fine-tuning the LLM on your prompt. The network's ordinary parameters stay frozen at inference. Only the small per-layer weights $W$ change, they start from $W_0$ for every sequence, and they are discarded afterwards, just like an RNN's hidden state.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: One lock, many cores: why a shared slab cache stops scaling
md: A shared lock caps allocator throughput at $1/c$ no matter how many cores you add. The fix is not a faster lock but keeping the common path on state that only one CPU (or thread) touches, and going to shared state rarely and in batches.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Stacking: let the rare thing rise to the top
md: Rare is not malicious and common is not safe. PEAK: "Just because something is abnormal doesn't mean it's malicious." And an attacker who pushes the same tool to every machine at once (ransomware deployment through a management tool, a compromised software update) is not rare at all. Stacking finds the start of an intrusion well and its widespread final stage poorly.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Collection: where intelligence comes from, and what it is worth
md: Collect against requirements, prefer sources about you (internal telemetry, sector peers), and measure every external source by what it contributes: relevance, timeliness and unique hits, not volume. For a question like PIR-1, check CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue from *Security from zero* first.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Attribution: levels, evidence and its limits
md: Technical evidence shows *what* and often *where*: tools, infrastructure, keyboard layouts, working hours. It rarely shows *who pays*. Be wary of attribution that rests on one artefact, on a tool many groups use, or on a country's motive alone, and never copy another vendor's attribution into your report without its confidence and basis.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Ranking threats: risk, DREAD and why it fell out of favour
md: Ranking is a conversation, not a calculation. Use a simple scale, write down the reasons behind each rating, and make sure every threat ends with an explicit response: mitigate, eliminate, transfer or accept.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Promotion: finding hot pages trapped in slow memory
md: Promotion needs two signals: *is this page hot* (recency of access) and *can we afford to move it* (free space, rate limit). Missing either one turns tiering into a migration storm.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: What TLS promises, and what it does not
md: TLS gives you an encrypted, tamper-evident channel to **whoever holds the private key for a certificate naming that host**. Everything else (is that the right host, is the CA trustworthy, is the code bug-free) is a separate question.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: HSTS, preloading and why key pinning fell out of favour
md: Mobile apps still pin. If you pin, pin to more than one key (RFC 7469 itself required a backup pin), prefer pinning a CA or intermediate key you control over a leaf, have a way to ship new pins before old keys retire, and remember that pinning cannot help against bugs like goto fail, where the chain is genuine but the handshake signature is never checked.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Autotuning, num_warps, num_stages and when to use Triton
md: Triton moves the hard parts of a CUDA kernel (coalescing, shared memory, barriers, pipelining) into the compiler, and leaves you the decisions that need knowledge of the problem: the tiling, the program-to-tile order, the masks, and a short list of configs to autotune.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: One app, two isolation layers: why a whole OS is redundant
md: A unikernel is **one application plus only the OS code it uses, linked into one image that boots directly on a hypervisor**. The hypervisor, not a guest kernel, is the isolation boundary.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Paravirtual I/O up close: one packet through a virtqueue
md: A virtqueue is **three shared arrays and two counters**. Data moves through memory for free; only **notifications** cost VM exits and interrupts, so batching, suppression and polling set the price of each packet.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
md: Deleting from hnswlib with `markDelete` only sets a flag. The node keeps its edges and is still used for routing; it is just filtered out of results. Lots of deletions therefore still cost traversal time until the index is rebuilt.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: 3D-HybridEngine: resharding the actor with zero redundancy
md: The paper describes the mechanism; today's code path is different in detail. With `actor_rollout_ref.hybrid_engine: true`, verl colocates actor and rollout, and the rollout is a vLLM or SGLang server with its own TP. After generation it sleeps (frees KV cache and weights); `update_weights` then wakes the weight memory, streams parameters tensor by tensor from the training engine, and finally restores the KV cache.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Tokenizing video and attending in space, then in time
md: In an ST-transformer the dominant cost, spatial attention, scales **linearly** with the number of frames instead of quadratically. That is what lets Genie use spatiotemporal context in the tokenizer, the latent action model and the dynamics model.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: The recipe: schedule, augmentation, per-layer learning rates
md: Augmentation is a training-time tool. At evaluation use only the checkpoint's deterministic resize, center crop and normalization; random crops or Mixup at test time just add noise to your accuracy estimate.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Why a transformer wants an image as a few discrete tokens
md: A visual tokenizer is to images what BPE is to text: a fixed map from raw input to a short sequence of ids from a finite vocabulary. Unlike BPE it is a learned, lossy neural network, so its reconstruction quality caps how good generated images can look.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: How vLLM chooses a backend: priority lists and validation
md: Automatic selection takes the first backend in the platform's priority list that passes `validate_configuration`. Explicit selection validates one backend and fails loudly. Neither path guesses.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Small text needs pixels: AnyRes tiling and dynamic resolution
md: Resolution is the main lever for reading text. Fixed-size models downscale, AnyRes adds tiles up to a grid limit, and dynamic-resolution models spend tokens in proportion to pixels. In every case more legible pixels means more visual tokens.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Consensus numbers: which primitives can build wait-free objects
md: The hierarchy is about deterministic wait-free algorithms. Herlihy notes that if the guarantee may be probabilistic (finite *expected* steps), the hierarchy collapses: randomized consensus from atomic registers exists. And a high consensus number says nothing about speed; it only says what is possible.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Scoring a forecast: latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC
md: RMSE rewards hedging. A smooth forecast that predicts the average of possible futures can beat a sharp, realistic one on RMSE while looking nothing like real weather. Read RMSE wins alongside ACC, spectra (how much variation a field has at each spatial scale; a blurry forecast is missing the small scales) or probabilistic scores.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Beyond port 443: what FTP, SMB, SNMP, LDAP and SMTP give away
md: Enumeration is asking questions a stranger should not get answers to. Use safe scripts, get written approval for intrusive ones, and pair every answer with its configuration fix: anonymous off, signing required, SNMPv3, VRFY disabled.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Case: Uber 2016, when a bug bounty was used to hide a breach
md: Authorisation is judged at the moment of access. A policy published afterwards, an NDA or a bounty payment cannot make earlier unauthorised access legal, for the person who took the data or for the company that tries to relabel it.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: CORS: how a server opts in to cross-origin reads
md: CORS is enforced by **browsers**, about **reading**. It is not access control on your server. `curl` or a script outside a browser ignores it completely, and a simple request reaches your server even when the browser will later hide the response. Authentication and authorization still have to happen on the server for every request.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Accounts, groups and SIDs: how Windows names every identity
md: SIDs, not names, are what Windows checks. A renamed Administrator still has RID 500, and a deleted and re-created account gets a new SID, so it does not inherit the old account's permissions.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WPA2: from passphrase to PMK to the 4-way handshake
md: Messages 1 and 2 move the nonces; messages 3 and 4 deliver the group key and confirm the keys, which is also how the handshake protects against downgrades. The PMK itself never crosses the air, but everything else that goes into the PTK does.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Mobile app storage: secrets on disk and in the package
md: Obfuscating a hardcoded secret (splitting it, XORing it, hiding it in native code) only slows an analyst down; the app must reconstruct it to use it, so an attacker with the app can too. If a value must stay secret from users, it must not be in the app.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Parking idle workers without lost wakeups or thundering herds
md: The searching count throttles wakeups, and the barrier on both sides of it prevents lost ones. Remove the throttle and you get a thundering herd; remove the barrier and you get stranded tasks with idle cores.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: Where the copies go in a read and write loop
md: Zero-copy does not mean faster for every request. It removes per-byte work but adds per-call and per-page bookkeeping. For small messages the copy is cheap and the bookkeeping can cost more, as lesson 5 measures.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: NLI entailment: is the label a true statement about the text?
md: A multi_label score near 0.6 is not a 60% chance the label applies. It is the entailment share after throwing away the neutral mass, from a model trained on MNLI sentence pairs, not on your labels. Treat it as a ranking score and set thresholds on labeled data.
